The Persuasion Gradient: Measuring Influence Operations at Scale

A research proposal submitted to the Meridian Foundation
(fabricated fixture document — every person, work, and finding is invented)

1. Background

Large-scale influence campaigns have shifted from broad demographic
targeting to individually tailored persuasion (Vance, 2019). Recent
work suggests that model-generated arguments can shift policy opinions
by measurable margins (Okafor & Lindqvist, 2022). Smith (2021) argued
that "durable attitude change requires repeated exposure across
multiple framings" and that single-shot interventions decay within
days. These findings extend earlier inoculation results (Smith, 2021;
Vance, 2019).

2. Prior Work

Delacroix et al. (2023) report that prebunking interventions retain
"roughly sixty percent of their measured effect ... eight weeks after
the final exposure" in platform-scale trials. The strongest critique
of this line of work holds that laboratory effects rarely survive
contact with platform dynamics (Marlowe, 2018). Field replications
remain scarce (see Okafor & Lindqvist, 2022, p. 14).

References

Delacroix, M., Ibarra, S., & Chen, W. (2023). Prebunking at platform
scale: A field experiment. Journal of Applied Misinformation Studies,
14(2), 101-129. https://doi.org/10.1234/jams.2023.0142

Okafor, C., & Lindqvist, A. (2022). Tailored persuasion and the limits
of microtargeting. Political Communication Quarterly, 9(4), 55-83.
https://doi.org/10.5678/pcq.2022.0904

Smith, J. (2021). Inoculation theory in synthetic media environments.
arXiv:2107.04321.

Vance, R. (2019). The demographic targeting fallacy. Meridian Press.
